followUps:
Data that must always be exactly right, data that is rarely read twice, and data that is cheap to fetch anyway.

Examples: account balances and stock counts at checkout (a stale read can oversell or overdraw), one-off reports read once (they only push useful keys out), and tiny lookups the DB already serves from its own memory in 1 ms. Be careful with personal data in a shared cache too: a key without the user id can show one user another user's page. Rule of thumb: cache when reads outnumber writes by about 10 to 1 and a few seconds of staleness is harmless.

At every hop of the request: browser, CDN, API gateway or reverse proxy, inside the app process, a shared cache such as Redis, and the database itself.

  • Browser and CDN: static files and public pages, closest to the user.
  • In-process (L1): about 100 ns, but each server holds its own copy.
  • Redis or Memcached (L2): about 0.5 ms, shared by all servers.
  • DB buffer pool: hot pages kept in RAM.

The closer to the user, the faster it is, but the harder it is to invalidate.

code.title: Cache-aside: hit, miss and delete-on-write
code.python:
db = {"u1": "Ann", "u2": "Bob"}   # source of truth
cache = {}                        # the cache (a real one also has a TTL)
db_reads = 0

def get(key):
    global db_reads
    if key in cache:              # hit: no DB work
        return cache[key], "hit"
    db_reads += 1                 # miss: read DB, then fill the cache
    cache[key] = db.get(key)
    return cache[key], "miss"

def update(key, value):
    db[key] = value               # 1) write the DB first
    cache.pop(key, None)          # 2) then delete the key; next read reloads

for k in ["u1", "u1", "u2", "u1"]:
    print("get", k, get(k))
update("u1", "Zed")
print("update u1 -> Zed")
print("get u1", get("u1"))
print("get u1", get("u1"))
print("DB reads:", db_reads, "of 6 gets")

followUps:
Deleting is safer, because two racing writers can leave the cache holding the older value, while a delete simply forces the next read to reload from the DB.

Example: writer A sets 5 and writer B sets 7, and the DB sees A then B. If the cache updates arrive B then A, the DB says 7 but the cache says 5 until the TTL. With deletes, both just remove the key and the next read loads 7. Deleting also avoids work nobody needs: if a row changes 100 times between reads, you do 100 cheap deletes and one rebuild.

The cache keeps serving the old value until its TTL runs out, so the TTL is your safety net and every key needs one.

Better: retry the delete, and if it still fails put the key on a queue (or let CDC from the DB log re-send it) so a background worker keeps trying. Example: with a 60 s TTL, staleness is capped at 60 s even if every delete is lost. Also delete after the DB commit, not before: deleting first lets a concurrent reader reload the old row and re-cache it.

code.title: Write-through vs write-around vs write-back
code.python:
class Store:
    def __init__(self, mode):
        self.mode, self.cache, self.db, self.db_writes, self.dirty = mode, {}, {}, 0, set()
    def write(self, k, v):
        if self.mode == "through":      # cache and DB together
            self.cache[k] = v; self.db[k] = v; self.db_writes += 1
        elif self.mode == "around":     # DB only, drop the cached copy
            self.db[k] = v; self.db_writes += 1; self.cache.pop(k, None)
        else:                           # back: cache only, flush later
            self.cache[k] = v; self.dirty.add(k)
    def flush(self):
        for k in self.dirty:
            self.db[k] = self.cache[k]; self.db_writes += 1
        self.dirty.clear()

for mode in ["through", "around", "back"]:
    s = Store(mode)
    for i in range(1, 6):               # 5 updates to the same counter
        s.write("views", i)
    before = dict(s.db)
    if mode == "back":
        s.flush()                       # one batched write
    print(mode.ljust(8), "DB writes:", s.db_writes,
          "| DB before flush:", before, "| in cache:", s.cache)
s = Store("back")
s.write("views", 99)
s.cache.clear()                         # cache crashes before the flush
print("back + crash: DB has", s.db, "-> update 99 is lost")

followUps:
Make the buffered writes durable and flush them quickly, so a cache crash loses little or nothing.

  • Append each write to a log (WAL) or a queue such as Kafka before acknowledging, and replay it after a crash.
  • Replicate the cache entry to a second node before acking.
  • Flush on a short timer or after N dirty entries, for example every 1 s or 500 entries.
  • Use it only for data that can be rebuilt, such as counters.

With a 1 s flush, a crash loses at most about 1 s of updates. Never use it for payments.

No. Two separate systems cannot be updated in one step, so a crash or timeout between the two writes leaves them disagreeing.

Example: the DB write succeeds but the cache write times out, so the cache keeps the old value. Or the cache write succeeds and the DB write fails, so the cache shows data that was never saved. The usual fix is to write the DB first (the source of truth), then update or delete the cache, with a TTL and retries as a safety net. For a real guarantee you need one transactional store or an outbox.

code.title: LRU cache: hash map plus doubly linked list
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, k=0, v=0):
        self.k, self.v, self.prev, self.next = k, v, None, None

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap, self.map = cap, {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()      # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head
    def _unlink(self, n):
        n.prev.next, n.next.prev = n.next, n.prev
    def _front(self, n):                           # most recent sits after head
        n.next, n.prev = self.head.next, self.head
        self.head.next.prev = n
        self.head.next = n
    def get(self, k):                              # O(1)
        n = self.map.get(k)
        if n is None:
            return -1
        self._unlink(n); self._front(n)
        return n.v
    def put(self, k, v):                           # O(1)
        n = self.map.get(k)
        if n:
            n.v = v; self._unlink(n); self._front(n); return
        if len(self.map) == self.cap:              # evict least recent (before tail)
            last = self.tail.prev
            self._unlink(last); del self.map[last.k]
        n = Node(k, v); self.map[k] = n; self._front(n)

c = LRU(2)
print("capacity=2")
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
print("get 1 ->", c.get(1))
c.put(3, 3)
print("get 2 ->", c.get(2))
c.put(4, 4)
print("get 1 ->", c.get(1))
print("get 3 ->", c.get(3))
print("get 4 ->", c.get(4))

followUps:
Store an expiry time in each node, treat an expired entry as a miss when it is read, and also sweep expired entries in the background.

Steps: 1) on put, set expiresAt = now + ttl; 2) on get, if now is past expiresAt, remove the node and report a miss; 3) optionally keep a min-heap of expiry times, or sweep a few entries per second, so unread entries do not hold memory. The lazy check is O(1); the heap adds O(log N) per put.

Node n = map.get(k);
if (n == null || n.expiresAt <= now()) {
  if (n != null) remove(n);
  return MISS;
}
moveToFront(n); return n.value;

LinkedHashMap is the same hash map plus doubly linked list, already built into one Java class.

Create it with accessOrder=true and every get or put moves the entry to the end of its list (most recent). Override removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity and the oldest entry is dropped automatically after an insert. About 5 lines give an LRU with O(1) get and put. It is not thread-safe: wrap it with Collections.synchronizedMap or use a lock.

new LinkedHashMap<K,V>(16, 0.75f, true) {
  protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K,V> e) {
    return size() > CAP;
  }
};

code.title: LRU vs LFU when a scan flushes the cache
code.python:
from collections import OrderedDict

def run(policy, trace, cap=3):
    cache, freq, tick, hits = OrderedDict(), {}, 0, 0
    last = {}
    for k in trace:
        tick += 1
        if k in cache:
            hits += 1
        elif len(cache) == cap:
            if policy == "LRU":
                victim = next(iter(cache))                 # least recently used
            else:                                          # LFU: lowest count, oldest use
                victim = min(cache, key=lambda x: (freq[x], last[x]))
            del cache[victim]; del freq[victim]
        cache[k] = True; cache.move_to_end(k)
        freq[k] = freq.get(k, 0) + 1
        last[k] = tick
    return hits

hot = ["A", "B", "C"] * 3                  # popular keys, used often
scan = ["X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "X5"]      # one-off scan, each key used once
after = ["A", "B", "C"]                    # popular keys come back
trace = hot + scan + after
print("trace:", " ".join(trace))
for p in ["LRU", "LFU"]:
    print(p, "hits on the final A B C:",
          run(p, trace) - run(p, hot + scan), "of 3")

followUps:
It evicts the item whose next use is furthest in the future. That gives the best possible hit rate, but it needs to know the future, so it cannot run live.

It is used as a yardstick: replay a recorded trace, compute Bélády's hit rate, and see how close LRU or LFU come. Example: cache of 2 holding A and B, then C arrives. If A is used next and B never again, evict B (LRU might evict A). If LRU gets 70% and Bélády gets 75% on your trace, there is little left to gain from a smarter policy.

Record real access traces and replay them through each policy at the cache size you plan to run, then compare hit rates.

Steps: 1) log key and time for a day or a week, including peaks and batch jobs; 2) simulate LRU, LFU and W-TinyLFU at a few sizes; 3) pick the best hit rate, and check byte hit rate if object sizes vary; 4) re-check after launch with real metrics. If the trace has scans (a nightly export), prefer an LFU-like or W-TinyLFU policy. If a policy wins by only 1%, take the simpler one.

code.title: Cache stampede: 20 requests, with and without single-flight
code.python:
import threading, time

db_loads = 0
def slow_db_load(key):
    global db_loads
    db_loads += 1
    time.sleep(0.1)                         # an expensive query
    return "value-of-" + key

def run(use_single_flight):
    global db_loads
    db_loads, cache, lock = 0, {}, threading.Lock()
    barrier = threading.Barrier(20)         # 20 requests arrive together
    def request():
        barrier.wait()
        if "hot" in cache:
            return
        if use_single_flight:
            with lock:                      # one loader per key; others wait
                if "hot" not in cache:      # re-check after getting the lock
                    cache["hot"] = slow_db_load("hot")
        else:
            cache["hot"] = slow_db_load("hot")
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=request) for _ in range(20)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    return db_loads

print("hot key just expired, 20 concurrent requests")
print("no protection  -> DB loads:", run(False))
print("single-flight  -> DB loads:", run(True))

followUps:
The lock has an expiry (TTL), so it frees itself and the next request can take over.

Example: SET lock:k id NX PX 3000. If the holder dies at t = 0.5 s, nobody can refill until t = 3 s, so waiting clients should serve a stale value or read the DB directly in the meantime. Choose the TTL a little above the normal load time (for example 3 times p99): too long and everyone waits after a crash, too short and two clients load at once.

Each request rolls a dice that says 'refresh now' more and more often as expiry gets closer, so one early refresh happens before the key expires instead of a crowd after it.

Rule: refresh if now - delta * beta * ln(rand) >= expiry, where delta is how long the load takes and rand is in (0,1). ln(rand) is negative, so subtracting it pushes 'now' forward by a random head start. Example: delta = 2 s, beta = 1: most requests refresh only within a few seconds of expiry, and slower loads start earlier. No locks or coordination are needed.

code.title: Bloom filter blocks lookups for keys that do not exist
code.python:
import hashlib, math

n, p = 1000, 0.01
m = math.ceil(-n * math.log(p) / math.log(2) ** 2)   # bits needed
k = round(m / n * math.log(2))                        # hash functions
bits = bytearray(m)

def positions(key):
    for i in range(k):                                # k hashes from sha256
        h = hashlib.sha256((str(i) + key).encode()).digest()
        yield int.from_bytes(h[:8], "big") % m

def add(key):
    for pos in positions(key):
        bits[pos] = 1

def maybe_has(key):                                   # False means definitely absent
    return all(bits[pos] for pos in positions(key))

for i in range(n):
    add("user:" + str(i))
print("n =", n, "target p =", p, "-> bits m =", m, ", hashes k =", k)
print("present keys found:", sum(maybe_has("user:" + str(i)) for i in range(n)), "of", n)
fp = sum(maybe_has("ghost:" + str(i)) for i in range(10000))
print("absent keys wrongly 'maybe present':", fp, "of 10000")
print("so about", 10000 - fp, "bogus lookups never reach the DB")

followUps:
About 120 MB with 7 hash functions, roughly 9.6 bits per key.

Bits m = -n ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 = 100M x 4.605 / 0.4805, which is about 959M bits, or about 120 MB. Hash count k = (m/n) ln 2 = 9.6 x 0.693, about 7. The filter answers 'maybe present' or 'definitely absent', so about 1% of absent keys still reach the DB and 99% are stopped. It cannot delete keys; use a counting filter or rebuild it.

Fill it before traffic arrives, loading the keys you know will be hot instead of letting users cause the misses.

  • Replay the top keys from yesterday's access log or a hot-key list.
  • Run a loader on deploy, throttled (say 1,000 keys/s) so the DB is not overloaded.
  • Bring new cache nodes in slowly by sending them a small share of traffic first.
  • Add jitter to TTLs so warmed keys do not all expire together.

Warm only the top few percent: caching the top 10% of keys often covers 85 to 95% of reads.

It splits the key space into 16,384 hash slots, and each master node owns a range of slots.

Slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. Example: with 3 masters, node 1 may own slots 0-5460, node 2 slots 5461-10922 and node 3 the rest. Clients cache the slot map and are redirected with MOVED when it changes. Keys used together in one command or Lua script must share a slot, so use a hash tag in braces, such as user:{42}:cart and user:{42}:profile, where only '42' is hashed. Resharding moves slots, not the whole data set.

A replica is promoted to master, but because replication is asynchronous, the last few writes that had not reached it are lost.

Steps: the nodes (or Sentinel) agree the master is unreachable after a timeout (say 5 s), the replica with the most data is elected and takes over the slots, and clients refresh their map. Expect a few seconds of errors and perhaps 1 s of lost writes. For a cache that is fine, since lost keys are just misses, but expect a burst of misses on the DB afterwards, so protect it.

A slow reader can put an old value into the cache after a writer already deleted the key, and that old value then stays until the TTL.

Timeline: 1) reader R misses and reads the DB, getting 1; 2) writer W updates the DB to 2; 3) W deletes the cache key; 4) R, delayed, sets cache = 1. Now DB = 2 and cache = 1. Fixes: a lease token (R's set is refused because the delete cancelled its token), a version number with compare-and-set, or a short TTL to limit the damage.

A daemon tails the database commit log in each region and sends deletes to that region's caches, so invalidation follows what really committed.

The tool is called McSqueal. Deletes go through routers that batch them. A region's caches are invalidated only after that region's replica has the change, so a reload cannot pull the old row from a lagging replica. For the writer's own reads, a remote marker says 'read from the primary region until replication catches up'.

code.title: Sizing a cache from a Zipf popularity curve
code.python:
N = 1_000_000                       # distinct keys
H = [0.0] * (N + 1)                 # H[c] = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/c (Zipf, s = 1)
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    H[i] = H[i - 1] + 1.0 / i

peak_qps, db_qps = 50_000, 5_000
need = 1 - db_qps / peak_qps
print("required hit rate = 1 - %d/%d = %.0f%%" % (db_qps, peak_qps, need * 100))
for pct in [1, 5, 10, 20]:
    c = N * pct // 100
    print("cache top %2d%% of keys -> hit rate %.1f%%" % (pct, H[c] / H[N] * 100))
c = next(c for c in range(1, N + 1) if H[c] / H[N] >= need)
print("smallest cache for the target: %d keys (%.1f%% of keys)" % (c, c / N * 100))
per_key = 40 + 500 + 80             # key + value + overhead, bytes
mem = c * per_key * 1.3 * 2         # headroom 1.3, 2 replicas
print("memory: %.0f MB incl. headroom and 2 replicas" % (mem / 1e6))

followUps:
Because DB load depends on the miss rate, and going from 99% to 98% hits doubles the misses.

Example: 100,000 reads/s. At 99% hits the DB gets 1,000/s; at 98% it gets 2,000/s; at 95% it gets 5,000/s. If the DB handles 1,500/s, losing one point of hit rate breaks it. So at high hit rates, size for the miss rate (1 minus hit rate) and leave headroom for dips.

Replay a real access trace through the cache at several sizes and plot miss ratio against cache size.

Steps: 1) collect a trace of keys (and sizes); 2) run it through an LRU simulator at sizes such as 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 GB; 3) plot the miss ratio for each. Pick the knee where more memory stops helping. A one-pass method (Mattson stack distances, or sampled tools like SHARDS) gives the whole curve in one scan: for each access, count the distinct keys touched since that key was last used; the access is a hit for any cache larger than that distance.

Count requests per key over a short window and flag keys that sit far above the rest.

Ways: sample about 1% of requests in the client and keep a top-K counter (a count-min sketch plus a small heap); Redis can list hot keys with redis-cli --hotkeys when an LFU policy is on; proxies can count per key. Example: the average key gets 10 req/s and one gets 50,000 req/s, so flag it, then serve it from L1 or split it into copies key#1 to key#8. The cost is small memory on each app server.

Up to the L1 TTL after Redis is correct, and up to about L1 TTL plus Redis TTL if L1 copies a value that is already stale.

Example: L1 TTL 5 s, Redis TTL 60 s. An entry deleted from Redis can still be served from L1 for up to 5 s. If invalidation messages are lost and Redis also holds an old value, a server may keep old data for several L1 cycles until the 60 s Redis TTL ends. So keep the L1 TTL to seconds and keep strict data out of L1.

A fencing token is a number that grows with each lock grant, and the protected resource rejects any write that carries an older number.

Example: A gets token 33, then stalls past its lock expiry. B gets token 34 and writes. When A wakes and writes with 33, the store sees 33 < 34 and refuses. This stops a slow ex-holder from corrupting data, which a TTL alone cannot. It needs the resource to check tokens, and for plain cache fills it is usually overkill.

Because it depends on clocks and timing that real systems do not guarantee, so critics say it is unsafe when you need correctness.

Redlock takes the lock on 5 independent Redis nodes and needs a majority (3). Critics note that a long GC pause or a clock jump can let a holder keep working after its lock expired, and Redlock gives no fencing token. It is fine for efficiency locks (avoiding duplicate work). For correctness use a consensus system such as ZooKeeper or etcd, with fencing tokens.

Rehashing pushes the dead server's whole load onto the others at once, and the burst of misses can overload the DB and knock over more servers (a cascading failure).

Meta instead sends that traffic to a small, idle gutter pool. Example: one of 100 servers dies, so its 1% of keys miss once into the gutter and stay cached there for a short TTL. The DB sees a small, bounded load. If the server was only briefly down, its keys come back with no mass reshuffle.

A remote marker is a small flag set when you write from a replica region, telling later reads of that key to go to the primary region until replication catches up.

Steps: 1) set a marker for the key in the local region and delete the local cache key; 2) send the write to the primary region's DB; 3) a read that finds the marker queries the primary region (slower but fresh) instead of the possibly lagging local replica; 4) the marker is removed when the replicated invalidation arrives. Result: read-your-writes at the cost of one cross-region read.

Sample cache hits and check, by a human or a stronger model acting as judge, whether the cached answer is right for the new question. The share of wrong ones is your false-hit rate.

Example: sample 200 hits a day and the grader marks 6 as wrong, so the false-hit rate is 3%. Also keep a labelled set of question pairs (same meaning or different meaning) and test the similarity threshold on it: raise the threshold until false hits fall under your target, say 1%, and accept a lower hit rate. Log each hit's similarity score so borderline cases can be reviewed.

Everything that can change the answer: the model and version, the prompt template version, the normalised input, and the settings that affect output.

  • Model name and version, plus temperature and other parameters (cache only when temperature is 0, or accept variety).
  • Prompt template version and a hash of the system prompt.
  • Normalised user input (trim, lowercase if safe).
  • Tenant, locale, and user or permission scope when the answer depends on them.
  • Versions of any retrieved documents.

Leaving one out causes wrong answers after a deploy or leaks between tenants.
